column2: - A file is one module, named on its first line of code. `##` comments describing it may come before.

- `main` lists the capabilities the program needs: here its arguments and the console. They are its whole authority. It can't touch files, the network or the clock, because it wasn't handed them (section 11).
- Blocks open with a keyword and close with `end`. Indentation carries no meaning; `mo format` lays code out with two spaces per level, in lines of at most 100 columns.

A program is a tree of modules under one root folder. The module `Shop.OrderBook` lives in `shop/order-book.mo`: each part of its name becomes a lowercase folder or file name, with hyphens between words. A word starts at a capital letter that follows a lowercase letter or a digit, and at the last capital of a run that a lowercase letter follows, so `XMLReader` lives in `xml-reader.mo`, `HTTP2Server` in `http2-server.mo` and `Unicode16Tool` in `unicode16-tool.mo`.

Source is UTF-8. Characters that change how text looks without being seen are an error anywhere, even in text and comments: direction overrides, zero-width characters, and control characters other than tab and line breaks. In text, write them as escapes, such as `"\u{200B}"`.

`#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. `##` documents the declaration below it, or the module when it comes before `module`. `mo format` lines up the comments at the ends of consecutive lines in one column, two spaces after the longest line's code.
- Values, functions, fields and parameters are snake_case: lowercase ASCII letters, digits and `_`, starting with a letter, or with `_` for a name that is unused on purpose.
- Types, the cases of choice types, and modules are CapCase: `OrderBook`, `NotFound`.
- A type parameter is a single capital letter: `T`, `K`, `V`.
- A name ending in `?` is a yes-or-no answer: a `Bool`, or a function that returns one, such as `empty?` or `paid?`.
- `_` alone means "ignored", and a name starting with `_`, such as `_reason`, is unused on purpose.
Names are ASCII; text and comments may use any Unicode. These words are reserved:
allows and assert break case continue else end enum examples expose false fn for forbids if implies in is module not or promise return stop struct test true try use var where while

A line break ends a statement; there are no semicolons. A statement continues on the next line when its line ends with an opening bracket, a comma, `.`, `=` or a binary operator, or when the next line starts with a closing bracket, `.`, `where` or a binary operator other than `-`. A statement also runs on through any block it opens, such as a `case` or an anonymous function written on several lines, to that block's `end`.

These show where a statement may break. `mo format` chooses the breaks itself: a statement that fits in 100 columns goes on one line, so it would join each of these, and a longer one is broken at its outermost brackets, dots or operators first. It counts columns as `Unicode16.display_width` does (section 14), turns any run of blank lines between statements into one, and writes no trailing commas.
| `Bool` | `true` and `false` | 3.1 |
| `Int`, `BigInt`, `Byte` | whole numbers | 3.2 |
| `Decimal`, `Float` | fractions | 3.3 |
| `Text`, `Char`, `Bytes` | Unicode text, one character, binary data | 3.4 |
| `Unit` | just `Unit`, what a function that returns nothing returns | 3.5 |
| `(A, B)` | tuples | 3.6 |
| `List(T)`, `Map(K, V)`, `Set(T)` | collections | 3.7, 3.8 |
| `Range` | whole numbers from `a` up to `b`, written `a..b` | 7.5 |
| `Time`, `Duration` | instants and lengths of time | 3.9 |
| records and choice types | declared with `struct` and `enum` | 4 |
| `fn(A) : B` | functions | 5.6 |
| `Option(T)`, `Result(T, E)` | maybe-missing values, and success or failure | 8 |
| capabilities | `Console`, `Files` and the others | 11 |

All values are immutable. A `var` (section 6.2) changes which value a name holds, never a value someone else holds. Mo never converts between types silently: a conversion is a function call, and one that could fail returns an `Option`. Conversions that round, such as `to_float` and `to_fixed`, say how they round. Comparing or combining values of different types is an error.
`and` and `or` evaluate their right side only when they need it, and `not` negates. A condition must be a `Bool`: no numbers, texts or lists stand in for one.
`a implies b` means `not a or b`. It reads best in promises (section 12.2).
`Int` is a 64-bit signed whole number, and the type of counts, sizes and positions. Literals may put `_` between digits, and may be hexadecimal or binary:

`+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `%` take two numbers of the same type. `/` rounds toward zero, and `%` gives the remainder with the sign of the left side: `-7 / 2` is `-3`, and `-7 % 2` is `-1`. `a.floor_div(b)` and `a.floor_mod(b)` round toward negative infinity instead.
Overflow, and dividing by zero, are bugs: the program stops. Code that expects a result might not fit says what it wants instead:

`BigInt` holds whole numbers of any size, with the same arithmetic: `n.to_big` converts to one, and `big.to_int` returns `None` when the value doesn't fit. `Byte` holds 0 to 255, for binary data; `n.to_byte` returns an `Option(Byte)`. `Byte` has no arithmetic (section 9.2): convert it with `to_int` first.

A literal with a decimal point, such as `19.99`, is a `Decimal`: an exact fraction with 18 decimal places, up to about ±1.7 × 10²⁰. Decimal arithmetic is exact while results fit in 18 places, so `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3`. A result that needs more places, such as `1.00 / 3`, is rounded to the nearest 18th place, with an exact tie rounded to the even digit. Overflow and dividing by zero stop the program, as with `Int`, and `%` gives the remainder with the sign of the left side, as it does for `Int`. A decimal's text form is its shortest exact spelling: `15.5`, `3`, `0.001`.

`Float` is a 64-bit IEEE 754 binary floating-point number, for science and graphics. A number literal takes the type its context needs: in `x * 0.5`, with `x` a `Float`, `0.5` is a `Float`, and in `price * 2`, with `price` a `Decimal`, `2` is a `Decimal`. A literal with nothing to decide its type is an `Int`, or a `Decimal` if it has a decimal point. Dividing an `Int` by an `Int` gives an `Int`, so convert first to get a fraction: `total.to_decimal / count.to_decimal`. Converting is explicit:

`Text` is Unicode text. It is stored as UTF-8 and is always valid. Text is written in double quotes, with the escapes `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\\`, `\"`, `\'`, `\#` and `\u{1F600}` (a character by its hexadecimal code). `#{...}` inside text inserts the text form of any value that has one (section 9.2), and may hold any expression, even one with text in it, as in `"#{name or "you"}"`. Lines inside `#{...}` break as they do elsewhere (section 2.4), with `#{` and its `}` as brackets, so a `case` may run over several lines there:

Text on several lines starts with `"""` at the end of a line and ends with `"""` first on a line, after its indentation; code may go on after it on that line, as in `""")`. It holds the lines between them, without the line break before the closing `"""`, which sets the indentation every line drops:
A `Char` is one Unicode character (a code point), in single quotes: `'a'`, `'\n'`, `'é'`.

Text has no single "length". `text.byte_count` counts UTF-8 bytes, instantly; `text.char_count` counts characters, reading the text. There is no `text[i]`: use whole-text operations such as `split`, `lines`, `trim`, `starts_with?` and `replace`, or walk `text.chars`. Two texts are equal when their bytes are equal, and texts sort by character code. Mo never normalizes text silently. The `Unicode16` module (section 14) normalizes text, splits it into user-perceived characters, and converts case beyond ASCII.
`Bytes` is binary data. `text.bytes` always succeeds; `bytes.decode_utf8` returns `None` when the bytes aren't valid UTF-8.
`Unit` is the type with one value, also written `Unit`. A function with no result type returns it. `Result(Unit, E)` is the result of an action that can fail but has nothing to return.
A tuple groups two or more values: `(3, "three")` has type `(Int, Text)`. `pair.0` and `pair.1` read its parts, and a pattern takes it apart:
`List(T)` is Mo's sequence: `[1, 2, 3]`, or `[]` when empty. Every element has the same type. Reading by position returns an `Option`, because the position may be past the end:

Functions that "change" a list return a new one, so `items.append(4)` on a line of its own is an error: the new list is unused. With a `var`, write `items = items.append(4)`. When the old list has no other holder, the new one reuses its memory, so building a list in a loop costs what it would with a mutable array (section 13.3).

`Map(K, V)` maps keys to values: `{"apples": 3, "pears": 5}`, or `{}` when empty. Keys are expressions, so `{fruit: 3}` uses the value of `fruit`. A literal that gives the same key twice is an error when the compiler can see it, as with two equal literals or the same name twice, and a bug when two keys turn out equal as the program runs. `Set(T)` holds distinct values: `Set.empty`, a constant, or `items.to_set`. Keys and set members need equality and hashing, which most types have (section 9.2).

Maps and sets keep insertion order, also after removals: iterating visits keys in the order they were added, setting an existing key keeps its place, and a key removed and added again goes last. Two maps are equal when they hold the same entries, in any order. Iterating a map gives `(key, value)` tuples.

A `Time` is an instant between the years 1 and 9999, read from a `Clock` (section 11). A `Duration` is a length of time, made from an `Int`: `5.seconds`, `200.milliseconds`, `3.minutes`, `2.hours`, `7.days`. Both count whole microseconds. Subtracting two times gives a `Duration`, and never overflows; adding a `Duration` to a `Time`, or subtracting one from it, gives a `Time`; durations add, subtract and multiply by an `Int`. A time outside the years 1 to 9999 is a bug, so `time.checked_add(duration)` returns an `Option`, `None` outside them, for code that can't rule it out; a negative duration goes back in time. Times and durations compare with `<` and the other comparisons.
A `struct` declares a record type: named fields, each with a type. A record is built by naming every field, in any order, and its fields are read with `.`:

When a record is built, its fields are computed in the order they are written there, whatever their order in the declaration. There are no optional fields; a field that may be missing has an `Option` type. Records have no methods: functions in the record's module work on it (section 5.4).
An `enum` declares a choice type: each value is exactly one of its cases. A case carries no data, one unnamed value, or named fields:
A case is built like a record, by naming its fields, or from its one unnamed value: `Circle(2.5)`. Types may be generic and recursive:

A module's cases share one name space: no two of its enums have a case of the same name, and no case reuses the name of a type or case that is always in scope, such as `Set`, `None` or `Error`. `Option` and `Result` are ordinary choice types (section 8).

A signature gives every parameter's type and the result's type; a function with no result type returns `Unit`. Inside a body, types are inferred from all their uses in it. A body is a sequence of statements, and its value is the value of its last line. `return` leaves early. A trailing `if`, a guard, is allowed only on the three early exits: `return`, `break` and `continue`.

Functions are declared at the top level of a module. There are no default or optional parameters. Two functions in a module share a name only when their first parameters are different types declared in that module, so both `Order` and `OrderLine` can have a `total`; a call picks the one whose first parameter matches.
Arguments are passed by position: `shipping(2.5, false)`. Only records and cases are built with named fields. A function with no parameters is called with empty parentheses: `defaults()`.

Functions may call themselves and each other. A call in tail position, the last thing a function does, takes the caller's place on the stack instead of adding to it, so a recursive loop can run as long as it needs to:

`x.f(a, b)` calls `f(x, a, b)`, and `x.f`, with no other arguments, calls `f(x)`: write `x.f`, not `x.f()`. Mo looks for `f` first in the module that declares the type of `x`, then among the names in scope. Chains read left to right: `text.trim.lines.size`.

Where a record's field and a function share a name, `x.name` is the field where the field is visible, and the function elsewhere (section 10.2). When the field holds a function, `x.name(a)` calls it with `a`.

`T.to_text(x)` is `x.to_text`, and `T.compare(a, b)` is `a.compare(b)`, for any type with `Text` or `Order` (section 9.2), including one that has it automatically. `T` is the type, as in `Text.compare(a, b)` or `Option.to_text(found)`, a type parameter, or the module that declares the type: `Shapes.to_text(shape)` takes any type `Shapes` declares. Without arguments they are function values, as in `shapes.map(Shape.to_text)`.
A single capital letter in a signature is a type parameter, and `where` asks for abilities (section 9):

A generic function can't call itself, directly or through other functions, with a type parameter standing for a bigger type built from that parameter. If `depth(t: Tree(T))` leads to a call of `depth` on a `Tree(List(T))`, `T` stands for `List(T)` there, and that is an error. Calling `depth` on a node's `left`, another `Tree(T)`, is fine. Each type a generic function is used with gets its own copy of the function, and such a call would need copies without end: for `Tree(List(T))`, `Tree(List(List(T)))`, and so on.

A named function is a value: `prices.map(with_tax)`. An anonymous function is written `fn(x) ... end`, on one line or several, and its parameter types are inferred. A function type is written like a signature: `fn(Decimal) : Decimal`, or `fn(Text)` for one that returns `Unit`.

An anonymous function can read names in scope where it is made, but it can't assign a `var` and can't capture a capability (section 11.4), so it can do only what its parameters allow; it may take a capability as a parameter. So printing each item works in a `for` loop, not inside `map`.

An anonymous function may read a `var` from the function around it only if nothing assigns that `var` after the anonymous function is made, including in a later round of a loop around it. Reading any other `var` is an error, since it would be unclear whether the function sees the value it was made with or a later one. Copy the value into a name first, and read the name:
To use a later value, make the function after the last assignment, or pass the value as a parameter.
`return` and `try` inside an anonymous function leave that anonymous function, not the function around it.

`name = value` binds a name once. A name is visible from its binding to the end of its block: a function's or a test's body, a branch of an `if`, an arm of a `case`, a loop's body, or an anonymous function's body.

Within a function or a test a name means one thing. While a local name, a parameter or a bound name, is visible it can't be bound again, even in an inner block or an anonymous function's parameters. So `line = line.trim` is an error: write `trimmed = line.trim`, or use a `var`. Separate blocks, such as two arms of a `case`, may use the same name. A function also can't refer to one of its module's functions or constants by a name it uses for a local: `fn open(owner: Text)` is fine in a module with an `owner` function, as long as `open` doesn't call `owner(...)`.
Unused names, parameters and imports are errors, and so is a result that isn't `Unit` and isn't used. A name starting with `_` is unused on purpose, and `for _ in 0..3` repeats without a name.
`var name = value` declares a name that can be assigned again within the function that declares it. Assigning to a field, or to a field of a field, builds a new record with that field changed:

`+=` and `-=` add to and subtract from a `var` or its fields; `mo format` writes `x = x + y` as `x += y`. Assignment never changes a value anyone else holds: whoever holds the old cart still sees the old cart. When the `var` is its value's only holder, the new value reuses its memory.
No parameter is passed by reference: a function returns a new value, and its caller assigns it.

`if` runs a block when its condition is true, with optional `else if` and `else` blocks. With an `else`, an `if` has a value: the value of the block that ran. A block `if` stands on a line of its own or after `=`.
A value that fits on one line uses the one-line form, which always has an `else` and may chain:

`case` compares a value with patterns, top to bottom, and runs the first arm that matches. An arm is `Pattern: statement` on one line, or `Pattern:` followed by lines that run until the next arm or `end`. The value of a `case` is the value of the arm that ran.

The arms must cover every possible value; if they don't, the error lists what's missing. When the value is a choice type, a whole arm can't be a catch-all, `_` or a name: list the cases, so that a case added later shows every place that must handle it. Inside a pattern, `_` and names may stand for anything, as in `Error(_)`. Arms with the same body share a line, as in `Saturday | Sunday: "weekend"`, and an arm may have a guard, as in `Some(n) if n > 10: "many"`.
| `_` | anything, and ignores it |
| `name` | anything, and binds it to `name` |
| `42`, `-1`, `2.5`, `"GET"`, `'x'`, `true` | that literal value |
| `None`, `Some(p)`, `Circle(p)` | that case, with its value matching `p` |
| `Rectangle(width: p, height: q)` | that case or record, with the named fields matching; fields not named are ignored |
| `(p, q)` | a tuple |
| `[]`, `[p, q]`, `[first, ..rest]`, `[first, .._]` | an empty list, a list of exactly two, and a list of at least one, with or without a name for the rest |

A case with named fields is matched by naming them, even when it has only one: `NotFound(path: p)`, or `NotFound(path: _)` to ignore the path. The form `Circle(p)` is only for a case's one unnamed value.

`value is Pattern` tests a pattern, giving a `Bool`. The names the pattern binds are visible where the test is known to be true: in the block of the `if` or `while` it guards, after `and` in the same condition, after `implies`, and after an `assert`.

`for` runs a block for each element of a list, set, map or range, and `while` runs a block while a condition is true. `break` leaves the loop, and `continue` starts its next round. A range `a..b` counts from `a` up to, but not including, `b`.
Mo has no null and no exceptions. A value that may be missing is an `Option`; a function that can fail returns a `Result`; and a bug stops the program (section 13.2). Both are ordinary choice types:

`x or default` gives the value inside a `Some`, or the default for `None`, and computes `default` only for `None`. `x.or_fail(e)` turns `None` into `Error(e)`; it is a function, so `e` is computed even when `x` is a `Some`. `case` and `is` handle both cases:
A function that can fail declares its failures as a choice type, and returns a `Result`:

`try expr` takes the value out of an `Ok`, or returns the `Error` from the function it is in. It works on a `Result` in a function that returns a `Result`, and on an `Option` in a function that returns an `Option`. In a function that returns neither, such as `main : Int` or a test, handle the failure with `case`. When the failure types differ, `try` wraps the failure if the function's failure type has exactly one case that holds it as its unnamed value, as `BadQuantity(QuantityError)` does:
With no such case, or more than one, `try` is an error that says which case to add. Ignoring a `Result` is an error too: every failure is passed upward or handled.
There is no "unwrap". Where a failure truly can't happen, the code says why, with `stop`:

Reaching a `stop` is a bug: the program stops and reports the reason. A `stop` fits wherever a value is expected, because control never comes back from it. So does a block or arm that ends in `return`: it leaves the function instead of giving a value.
`List(T)`, `Map(K, V)` and your own types take type parameters:

A generic type can't hold itself at a bigger type built from its parameter, as a `Tree(T)` with a field `children: List(Tree(List(T)))` would. Each type a generic type is used with becomes a type of its own, and that one would need types without end, as such a call would for a generic function (section 5.5). `children: List(Tree(T))` is fine.
An ability is something a type can do. There are five, all built in:
| `Equal` | `==` and `!=` | nothing: values are equal when their fields are |
| `Hash` | use as a map key or a set member | nothing: always structural |
| `Order` | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `sort`, `min` and `max` | `fn compare(a: T, b: T) : Ordering` |
| `Text` | a text form, for `#{...}` and printing | `fn to_text(x: T) : Text` |
| `Number` | `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` and `sum` | nothing: only `Int`, `BigInt`, `Decimal` and `Float` have it; times and durations also add and subtract (3.9) |

A type with `Hash` or `Order` also has `Equal`. Ability names appear only after `where`, so they don't clash with other names. Records and choice types get `Equal`, `Hash`, `Order` and `Text` automatically whenever all their fields have them. Equality compares field by field; maps compare their entries, and sets their elements, in any order. Order compares fields in the order they are declared, and cases in the order they are declared. Functions and capabilities have no abilities. The built-in types have these:
| `Bool` | yes | yes | `false` first | yes | no |
| `Int`, `BigInt`, `Decimal` | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `Byte` | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `Float` | IEEE: "not a number" equals nothing | no | yes, with "not a number" last | yes | yes |
| `Text`, `Char` | yes | yes | by character code | yes | no |
| `Bytes` | yes | yes | byte by byte | no | no |
| `Unit` | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `Time`, `Duration` | yes | yes | yes | yes | no (but they add and subtract, 3.9) |
| `Range` | yes | yes | no | yes: `0..3` | no |
| tuples | when every part has it | same | same, part by part from the left | same | no |
| `List(T)` | when `T` has it | same | same, element by element; a list comes before any longer list that begins with it: `[1, 2] < [1, 2, 0]` | same | no |
| `Map(K, V)`, `Set(T)` | when their keys and values have it, comparing entries in any order | same | no | same | no |

`Option`, `Result` and `Ordering` are choice types, so their cases are ordered as they are declared: `None`, `Some`; `Ok`, `Error`; `Less`, `Equal`, `Greater`. `Float` follows IEEE rules: "not a number" equals nothing and sorts last, and floats have no `Hash`, so they can't be map keys.

A value's text form looks like the code that builds it: `Point(x: 1.5, y: 2)`, `Some(3)`, `[1, 2]`, `{"a": 1}`, `(1, true)`, `[1, 2].to_set`. A `Text` or `Char` value's text form is itself; inside another value's, it is quoted and escaped as in code. Numbers have their shortest spelling. A `Float` is written in plain digits, as `1000` or `0.25`, unless its size is below 1e-6 or at least 1e21, when it has an exponent, as `1e21` or `1.5e-7`. A whole float has no `.0`, zero is `0` and negative zero `-0`, and a float that is not a number is `nan`, the infinities `inf` and `-inf`. A `Bool` is `true` or `false`, a `Time` is RFC 3339 text, and a `Duration` is in seconds, as `1.5s`. `x.to_text` gives the text form of any value whose type has `Text`: the same text as `"#{x}"`.
`x.compare(y)` compares two values whose type has `Order`, giving `Less`, `Equal` or `Greater`.
A type customizes `Order` or `Text` with one ordinary function in its own module, which applies wherever the type goes, exposed or not:
There are no user-defined abilities in v0.1. Code that needs something other than these five takes a function as a parameter.
A module starts with its name, then the `expose` line listing its public names, then its `use` lines:
Everything not on the `expose` line is private to the module. Tests in the same file see everything (section 12.3).

`expose Order` exposes the type without its fields or cases. Outside the module an `Order` can't be built, taken apart or have its fields read; it can only be passed to the module's functions. `expose OrderError(..)` exposes the fields or cases too. Hidden insides keep values valid: if `place` is the only way to get an `Order`, every `Order` has passed `place`'s checks.

`use Shop.Catalog` lets this module write `Catalog.find(...)` and `Catalog.Item`. `use Shop.Money{Money, add}` also brings those names in unqualified, and a choice type's exposed cases come with it. A module may declare a type with its own name, as the module `Account` declares `Account`: `Account.open(...)` calls the module's function, and `Account` in a type is the type. There are no wildcards and no aliases. A clash between names is an error that suggests the qualified form, and so is a cycle of modules that use each other. The library's modules, `Json` and `Unicode16`, are used the same way, and a program can't declare a module with one of their names.
A module may bind fixed values at its top level:

A constant's type comes from its value, which must decide it; for anything else, such as a list of anonymous functions, write a function with a signature. Constants are computed once, before any other code of the program runs, in the order of their dependencies. A constant depends on the constants it uses, directly or through the functions it calls. So a constant may use one written below it, or one in another module, but constants that depend on each other in a cycle are an error. A constant that stops stops the program before it starts. There is no module-level state: values that last and change belong to processes, which come in a later version.

Always in scope: the built-in types of section 3, `Option` with `Some` and `None`, `Result` with `Ok` and `Error`, `Ordering` with its cases, the capability types, `FileError` with its cases, and `Entry` with `EntryKind` and its cases. The functions of section 14 belong to their types' modules: call them with a dot, as in `text.lines`, or through the module, as in `Set.empty` and `Time.parse(text)`. So a local may be called `lines` or `count` without clashing with them.

A function can affect or observe the world outside the program only through capabilities it is handed as parameters. A capability's type names what it can do: `Console` prints, `Files` reads and writes files, `Clock` tells the time. So a function's parameter types are its complete list of effects, and a function with no parameter that is or holds a capability only computes: given the same arguments, it always gives the same result.
| `Args` | read its command-line arguments |
| `Env` | read environment variables |
| `Console` | print to standard output and standard error, and read standard input |
| `Files` | read and write files in one folder and the folders inside it |
| `ReadFiles` | only read them |
| `Clock` | read the current time |
| `Random` | draw random numbers |

`main` lists the capabilities the program needs, in any order and at most one of each type. The runtime hands over exactly those, so a program's whole authority is on its first line. The `Files` or `ReadFiles` it gets reach the folder the program was started in.

`main` returns nothing, and the program exits with status 0; or an `Int`, the exit status, from 0 to 255; or `Result(Unit, E)`, where `Error(e)` prints `e`'s text form to standard error and exits with status 1.

A capability can be narrowed before it is passed on. `files.within("reports")` reaches only that folder, and `files.read_only` returns a `ReadFiles`, which can only read. Calling `within` with a path that would leave the folder, such as `".."`, gives a capability that reaches nothing (section 14). Pass each function the least it needs:
- Records may hold capabilities, so a function that needs several can take one record.
- Anonymous functions can't capture capabilities, or values holding them. A function that needs one takes it as a parameter.
- Only the runtime makes real capabilities. Tests, examples and promises use fakes (section 12.4).
- Capabilities have no abilities: they can't be compared, printed or used as keys.
- There are no log statements. To report something, print it or return it.
A function's specification sits at the top of its body: its promises and examples, then a blank line, then its code.
`examples` lists calls with their expected results. Each line is a `Bool` expression, usually `call == expected`, and `mo test` checks every line:
A `promise` states what must hold for every call. It has three parts:
- **a sentence** saying, in plain words, what is promised;
- **a body**: one or more `Bool` lines over the parameters and `result`, the function's result, which must all be true;
- **anchors**: at least one `allows` line and one `forbids` line. Each gives every parameter and `result` a value, which the body must accept or reject.

The compiler checks that the body accepts every `allows` and rejects every `forbids`, which catches a body that doesn't say what its sentence says. `mo test` checks the body against the function on many generated inputs, boundaries first. It builds a type exposed without its insides only through a limited number of calls to its module's exposed functions, other types from any values of their fields, and capabilities as fakes. A promise speaks about calls that return; a call that stops on a generated input is reported as a bug, with the input. The boundaries include each type's extremes, such as `Decimal`'s largest value and the last instant of the year 9999, so a promise that passes holds for every call its types allow. When an extreme stops a call, the report says so, as in "stops with overflow when `amount` is `Decimal`'s largest value", and shows the two fixes: return a failure for such inputs, or take a type whose module keeps its values in range. Proofs come in a later version.

For a generic function, `mo test` checks every concrete instantiation already present in the program, including those supplied by anchors, examples and tests. It keeps each complete list of type arguments as used; it does not combine arguments from different uses or choose additional types. It generates and shrinks values separately for each instance, and a failure names its concrete types. This checks those instances, not every possible substitution for the function's type parameters.
A promise about many steps, such as "an accepted job is never lost", is a promise on the function that takes one step: something each step keeps true between its input and its result.
There are no preconditions. What a caller must guarantee becomes a type, such as a `Quantity` that its module never builds negative, or a failure, such as `Error(InvalidAmount)`.

A `test` names a scenario in a sentence and checks it with `assert`. Tests live in the same file as the code and see its private names. A name bound by `assert ... is Pattern` stays in scope for the rest of its block:

Tests, examples and promises make fake capabilities, which reach nothing outside the program: `Console.fake()`, whose `printed` and `printed_errors` list the lines written to standard output and standard error; `Console.fake_input(lines)`, which also has those lines to read; `Files.in_memory(files)`, from a map of paths to texts; `Clock.fixed(time)`; `Random.seeded(n)`; `Args.of(list)`; and `Env.of(map)`. Fakes are made only there, never in a module's constants or its functions. `printed` and `printed_errors` can be used only there too, where every console is a fake, and using them anywhere else is an error.

A capability is a handle on something outside the program, and a fake is a handle on something kept for the test. Every use of one fake sees the same files and the same output: a file that `main` writes to a `Files.in_memory(...)` fake can be read back, and a `Console.fake()` passed to `main` shows afterwards what `main` printed.

Mo evaluates eagerly, left to right: a call's arguments, then the call; an operator's left side, then its right. `and`, `or` and `implies` skip their right side when the left decides the answer, and `x or default` on an `Option` computes `default` only when `x` is `None`. `try` returns early, and `stop` stops the program.

A bug stops the program at once, with a report of what happened and where, and exit status 70. These are bugs: overflow in `Int`, `Decimal` or `Duration` arithmetic, or a time outside the years 1 to 9999; dividing by zero; reaching a `stop`; using more stack, call depth or memory than section 13.4's limits allow, or more memory than the machine has; calling a library function outside what it accepts, such as `take(-1)` or `random.int(5, 5)`; two keys of a map literal that turn out equal (section 3.8); an exit status outside 0 to 255; printing to an output that is gone; having too many folders open at once; and a fake whose files make one path both a file and a folder (section 14). Bugs are never caught.
Mo promises what operations cost, not how values are stored:
| `get`, `size`, `first` and `last` on a list | constant |
| `append` on a list, and assigning a `var`'s field | constant when the value has one holder; a copy when it's shared |
| `get` on a map, and `has?` on a map or a set | constant on average |
| `set` and `remove` on a map, and `add` and `remove` on a set | constant on average when the value has one holder; a copy when it's shared |
| `byte_count` | constant |
| `char_count`, `split`, `lines`, `contains?` | proportional to the text's length |
| `sort`, `sort_by` and `sort_by_desc` | n log n, and stable: equal keys keep their order |
A value is shared when two names, fields or collections hold it. Changing a value with one holder reuses its memory; changing a shared value copies it first, and its other holders keep the old value.

Each command is given the file of the program's main module; `mo check` and `mo test` also accept a library module. `mo check FILE` reports the program's errors, `mo run FILE [ARGS...]` runs it with the arguments after the file's name, and `mo test FILE` checks its examples, promises and tests. `mo emit FILE -o OUT` checks the program as `mo check` does and writes its bytecode to `OUT`; `-o` is required, and a library module has no main to emit (E0079). `mo format` and `mo fix` rewrite the files they are given. `mo guide` needs no file. It prints a short guide for agents writing Mo, matched to the installed version: how to work with the `mo` command, a small complete program with its tests, and when a task is done. `mo guide --reference` prints this reference. `mo` exits with status 0 when everything passed, 1 when the program has errors or an example, promise or test fails, and 2 for a mistake in the command itself. Once the program runs, `mo run` exits with the program's own status (section 11.2), or 70 after a bug (section 13.2).

`mo test` runs every example, promise and test unless it's told which. Each has a full name: its function's name, or a test's module's, then its kind and a number counted from 1 in source order, such as `Wc.count.example.3` for the third example of `Wc.count`, `Account.transfer.promise.1`, or `Wc.test.2` for the second test in `Wc`. `--only NAME` runs the one with that full name, and can be given more than once; `--in MODULE` runs one module's, still checking the whole program; and `--list` prints the full names without running anything. A selection that matches nothing is a mistake in the command.

`mo run` and `mo test` limit what a program uses: `--max-stack` sets the bytes of stack, by default 8 MiB; `--max-depth` the calls in progress at once, by default 10,000; and `--max-heap` the bytes of memory, by default 1 GiB. Going past one is a bug whose report names the limit (section 13.2). A call in tail position takes its caller's place on the stack and doesn't count toward the depth (section 5.3). A program can't set its own limits.

`mo check --json` and `mo test --json` write one JSON object per line to standard output: first the format's version, then one for each error and for each example, promise and test run, and last the totals and the exit status. Within a major version of the format, every field keeps its name, type and meaning, and an error's code keeps its meaning; new fields and new kinds of object may be added, so a reader skips what it doesn't know. A message's wording may change.

Each function is listed under the type of its first parameter, written as it is called with a dot: under **Text**, `split(separator: Text) : List(Text)` is called as `text.split(",")`. A function written `Type.name(...)` is called through the type's module. `pred` is a function returning a `Bool`. Calling a function outside what it accepts, such as `take(-1)`, is a bug (section 13.2). Every type with the `Text` ability also has `to_text : Text`, its text form, and every type with `Order` has `compare(other: T) : Ordering` (section 9.2).

Writing or appending into a folder that doesn't exist gives `Error(NotFound(path: path))`; `make_folder` makes the folder and any missing folders above it, and succeeds if the folder already exists. `entries(folder: Text) : Result(List(Entry), FileError)` gives the folder's entries in `list`'s order, each an `Entry(name: Text, kind: EntryKind)` whose kind is `File`, `Folder`, `Link` or `Other`; a link is reported, never followed. `walk(folder: Text) : Result(List(Entry), FileError)` gives every entry below the folder, each named by its path from the folder: a folder's entries in `list`'s order, each folder followed by what's inside it. It doesn't enter links, and stops at the first folder it can't read. A capability from `within` or `read_only` holds its folder open while it's used, and having too many open at once is a bug (13.2). `Files.in_memory(files: Map(Text, Text)) : Files`. In such a fake, the folders are those its files are in, those `make_folder` made, and those whose last file was removed, as on a disk, and `list` and `entries` give the names directly inside a folder, each subfolder once. Files that make one path both a file and a folder, as `{"a": "x", "a/b": "y"}` do, are a bug (13.2). So are keys that aren't plain relative paths, such as `"/a"`, `"./a"`, `"a/"` or `"a//b"`. **ReadFiles** has `read_text`, `read_bytes`, `list`, `entries`, `walk`, `exists?` and `within`. Paths are relative and use `/`; `"."` is the capability's own folder, and no path can leave it. Given a path that would leave the folder, such as `"../a.txt"`, reading, writing, removing and listing give `Error(NotAllowed(path: path))`, and `exists?` gives `false`. Calling `within` with such a path gives a capability that reaches nothing: every call on it that returns a `Result` gives `Error(NotAllowed(path: path))`, and `exists?` on it gives `false`. A path may pass through symbolic links that stay inside the folder, and every operation follows them; a path through an absolute link, or one that leads outside, is refused in the same way, and one through more than 40 links gives `Error(Failed(path: path, reason: "too many links"))`. `remove` removes a link itself, never what it points to. Listing a file, or making a folder where a file is, gives `Error(Failed(path: path, reason: "not a folder"))`, and reading, writing, appending to or removing a folder gives `Error(Failed(path: path, reason: "is a folder"))`.
